def.title: The Winter Market Takings
def.blurb: The Christmas market raises a record sum for the lifeboat. By morning, the takings tin has vanished from the village hall.

intro.text: The Christmas market. Lanterns, mince pies, carols, and the best day the lifeboat tin has ever had.
Over nine hundred pounds, my lover! I left the tin on the stage while we swept up. Ten o'clock, that was.
Next morning, the stage is bare. The tin is gone.
Wasn't the hall locked?
The back door lock's been broken for weeks. The council keeps saying next Tuesday.
Mrrp. (So anyone could walk in. We'll have to work out who couldn't.)

clue.title: The Empty Stage
clue.text: The tin was taken from the stage after the hall was swept at ten. The back door doesn't lock, so anyone could have come in.

intro.text: I judged the carol boats this year. Heaven help me, I agreed to it.
Then the judges came back to Gull Point for supper. Five of them, and they didn't leave until one.
Gull Point's a long walk from the village hall.
Mrow. (And five judges watching her carve a ham. No tin in the soup.)

clue.title: The Judges' Supper
clue.text: Morwenna judged the carol boats, then hosted the five judges for supper at Gull Point until one in the morning.

intro.text: Market night's my busiest night of the year. I didn't sit down till one.
Look at the till roll, if you like. Something rung up every few minutes, and my name on every one.
Ten twenty: two mulled wines. Ten twenty-three: a pie. Ten twenty-six: a lemonade and a pickled egg.
Mrrp. (A pickled egg every three minutes. Ned never left his bar.)

clue.title: The Till Roll
clue.text: The Anchor was packed until one. The till roll shows Ned ringing up drinks every few minutes all evening, under his own name.

intro.text: After we swept up, I took the lifeboat out to bring the carol boats home. Lanterns on every mast.
We were at sea till midnight, then cleaning her down till two. The crew were with me every minute.
It's in the escort log?
Mrow. (Every boat named, every time written down. Tamsin counts everything twice.)

clue.title: The Escort Log
clue.text: Tamsin took the lifeboat out to escort the carol boats home. The log has her at sea until midnight and cleaning down with her crew until two.

intro.text: Under the stage steps, Biscuit finds a scrap of blue paper, folded small.
It's the stub of a night-safe envelope. From the bank in Penmarrow.
Night-safe keys? Only businesses get those. There's two in Little Wending: mine, for the Anchor, and Rafe's.
Mrrp. (And who's been looking very shifty about his car since breakfast?)

clue.title: The Envelope Stub
clue.text: A night-safe envelope stub from the Penmarrow bank lay under the stage steps. Only business account holders have night-safe keys: Rafe, for his shop, and Ned, for the Anchor.

def.question: Who took the charity tin?

accusePrompt.text: Five clues, Biscuit. Who took the charity tin?
Mrrp. (Who wasn't at Gull Point, behind the bar, or out at sea, and has a night-safe key?)

tamsin.text: Mrow. (Tamsin was at sea and then cleaning down the lifeboat until two. The escort log says so.)

ned.text: Mrow. (Ned rang up a drink every few minutes until one. He never left the Anchor.)

morwenna.text: Mrow. (Morwenna had five judges to supper at Gull Point until one in the morning.)

ending.text: Rafe. It was you. You're the only one left with a night-safe key.
Guilty. I walked past at half ten. Nine hundred pounds in a biscuit tin, and a door that doesn't lock.
So I drove it to the night safe in Penmarrow. In the lifeboat's name. Here's the receipt.
Why on earth didn't you tell anyone?
Who'd believe the antiques dealer had been to the bank with their money? Be honest.
The bank confirms it: every penny of the takings, and two hundred pounds more, from Rafe's own pocket.
Well. I owe you a pint, Rafe Delacroix. Several.
Purrr. (Rafe was guilty of being kind. I didn't see that coming. Mince pies all round.)
Have you heard, Goldie? The council is lending the Kittiwake's figurehead to the museum in Penmarrow.

scene.alt: The village hall dressed for the Christmas market, lanterns in the windows and snow on the step
